title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 362
paragraphs: but I will now recount what other nations also tell, and what the Egyptians report in agreement with the others, about what happened in this land; and I will also add something of what I have seen myself.

Being set free after the reign of the priest of Hephaistos, the Egyptians, since they could not live any length of time without a king, set twelve kings over themselves, dividing all of Egypt into twelve parts. These kings intermarried with one another and reigned together, making agreements that they would not try to overthrow one another by force, nor seek any advantage over one another, but would live in perfect friendship. The reason they made these agreements and guarded them so strictly from being broken was this: an oracle had been given to them at the outset, when they first began to exercise their rule, that whichever of them poured a libation with a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos would become king over all Egypt — for they used to assemble together in all the temples.
